      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Psoriasis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">Psoriasis</span> is a skin disease that causes itchy or sore patches of thick, red skin with silvery scales. You usually get the patches on your elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms and feet, but they can show up on other parts of your body.  Some people who have <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span> also get a form of arthritis called <span class="qt0">psoriatic</span> arthritis.</p><p>A problem with your immune system causes <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span>. In a process called cell turnover, skin cells that grow deep in your skin rise to the surface. Normally, this takes a month. In <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span>, it happens in just days because your cells rise too fast. </p><p><span class="qt0">Psoriasis</span> can be hard to diagnose because it can look like other skin diseases. Your doctor might need to look at a small skin sample under a microscope.</p><p><span class="qt0">Psoriasis</span> can last a long time, even a lifetime. Symptoms come and go. Things that make them worse include:</p><ul><li>Infections</li><li>Stress</li><li>Dry skin</li><li>Certain medicines</li></ul><p><span class="qt0">Psoriasis</span> usually occurs in adults. It sometimes runs in families. Treatments include creams, medicines, and light therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases </p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/dandruffcradlecapandotherscalpconditions.html">
      <content name="title">Dandruff, Cradle Cap, and Other Scalp Conditions</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seborrheic Dermatitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seborrhea</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your scalp is the skin on the top of your head. Unless you have hair loss, hair grows on your scalp. Different skin problems can affect your scalp.</p><p>Dandruff is a flaking of the skin. The flakes are yellow or white. Dandruff may make your scalp feel itchy. It usually starts after puberty, and is more common in men. Dandruff is usually a symptom of seborrheic dermatitis, or seborrhea. It is a skin condition that can also cause redness and irritation of the skin.</p><p>Most of the time, using a dandruff shampoo can help control your dandruff. If that does not work, contact your health care provider.</p><p>There is a type of seborrheic dermatitis that babies can get. It is called cradle cap. It usually lasts a few months, and then goes away on its own. Besides the scalp, it can sometimes affect other parts of the body, such as the eyelids, armpits, groin, and ears. Normally, washing your baby's hair every day with a mild shampoo and gently rubbing their scalp with your fingers or a soft brush can help. For severe cases, your health care provider may give you a prescription shampoo or cream to use.</p><p>Other problems that can affect the scalp include:</p><ul><li>Scalp ringworm, a fungal infection that causes itchy, red patches on your head. It can also leave bald spots. It usually affects children.</li><li>Scalp <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span>, which causes itchy or sore patches of thick, red skin with silvery scales. About half of the people with <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span> have it on their scalp.</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/psoriaticarthritis.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Psoriatic</span> Arthritis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">Psoriasis</span> is a skin disease that causes itchy or sore patches of thick, red skin with silvery scales. You usually get them on your elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms and feet, but they can show up on other parts of your body.</p><p>Some people with <span class="qt0">psoriasis have psoriatic</span> arthritis.  It causes pain, stiffness, and swelling of the joints.  It is often mild, but can sometimes be serious and affect many joints. The joint and skin problems don't always happen at the same time.</p><p>Your doctor will do a physical exam and imaging tests to diagnose <span class="qt0">psoriatic</span> arthritis. There is no cure, but medicines can help control inflammation and pain. In rare cases, you might need surgery to repair or replace damaged joints.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ankylosingspondylitis.html">
      <content name="title">Ankylosing Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rheumatoid Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Spondylitis, Ankylosing</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis of the spine. It causes inflammation (swelling) between your vertebrae (the bones that make up your spine) and the joints between your spine and pelvis. AS inflammation can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</p><p>Symptoms of AS can range from mild to severe back pain. Over time, AS can fuse (grow together) your vertebrae, limiting movement and causing a hunched posture. In some people, AS can affect other joints or body parts.</p><p>There is no cure for AS, but early treatment can help manage symptoms, slow down the disease, and help you lead a more productive life.</p>Who is more likely to get ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis usually starts before age 45. Early symptoms may begin between the ages of 15 and 30. Your chance of developing AS can also increase if:</p><ul><li>You're a man. AS is more common and severe in men.</li><li>You have a family history. If a member of your family has AS, you're more likely to get the disease.</li><li>You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting AS. These include Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span>.</li></ul>What causes ankylosing spondylitis?<p>No one knows what causes ankylosing spondylitis, but the environment and genes likely play a role. Your genes are parts of DNA in your cells that are passed down from your parents. Certain genes may increase your risk of getting the disease, but not everyone with these genes gets AS.</p>What are the symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS affects people differently. The most common symptom is pain and stiffness in the lower back and/or hips. The pain is usually worse during the night or after sitting for a long time.</p><p>Over time, AS may progress to other areas of your spine or body. Symptoms may depend on which areas of your body the disease affects. Some people have symptoms that come and go. Others may have severe, ongoing pain.</p><p>Other symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, stiffness, and inflammation of the joints.</li><li>Difficulty taking a deep breath. This could occur if the joints connecting the ribs are affected.</li><li>Changes in vision.</li><li>Fatigue.</li><li>Loss of appetite.</li><li>Weight loss.</li><li>Skin rashes, such as <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span>.</li><li>Abdominal (belly) pain and loose stools (poop).</li></ul>How is ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed?<p>There is no single test for ankylosing spondylitis. To find out if you have AS your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had AS.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies.</li></ul>What are the treatments for ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS has no cure, but treatment may help relieve symptoms, maintain posture, and slow down the disease. Since other parts of your body can be affected by AS, you will likely work with a team of health care professionals for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p><p>Treatment usually includes medicine to help relieve symptoms and keep the disease from getting worse, as well as physical therapy to improve mobility. If AS is severe, surgery may be needed.</p><p>You can help manage your AS symptoms if you:</p><ul><li>Exercise</li><li>Monitor your symptoms</li><li>Manage your stress</li><li>Use assistive devices as needed</li><li>Follow a healthy diet</li><li>Stop smoking, or don't start</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Disease</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/arthritis.html">
      <content name="title">Arthritis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Joint inflammation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is arthritis?<p>If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee.</p><p>Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have.</p>What are the types of arthritis?<p>Common types of arthritis include:</p><ul><li>Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury.</li><li>Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake.  Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis.</li><li>Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children.</li><li>Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type.</li><li><span class="qt0">Psoriatic</span> arthritis affects people with <span class="qt0">psoriasis</span> (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches).</li><li>Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected.</li><li>Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of arthritis?<p>Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common arthritis symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever, weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash.</p><p>Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses.</p>Who is more likely to get arthritis?<p>A few things that might increase your chance of getting arthritis include:</p><ul><li>Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of arthritis if a member of your family has the disorder.</li><li>Age. The risk of getting many types of arthritis increases with age.</li><li>Sex. Certain types of arthritis are more common in women, while other types are more common in men.</li></ul><p>Other factors that might increase your risk of getting arthritis include having a previous joint injury, obesity, or lupus.</p>How is arthritis diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have arthritis, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or take x-rays.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in arthritis care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for arthritis?<p>Treatment depends on the type of arthritis you have. It may include medicine or surgery. Your provider will work with you to improve your symptoms and quality of life.</p><p>A few ways to help manage your symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Hot or cold packs</li><li>Relaxation techniques</li><li>Use of splints, braces, and/or assistive devices</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>
